instagram_caption:
🚀 The $111B SMS world didn’t just “decline”… it got replaced.

In 2011, global SMS messaging revenue still sat around **$111B**. That’s the size of an era: texting as the default communication layer, run through carriers, billed per message, embedded into every phone plan.

Then WhatsApp arrives into the smartphone age and slowly turns the dial. By **2013**, WhatsApp starts showing measurable value in this comparison (about **$0.8B** in the early ramp), but the real shock hits later: as smartphones spread and data plans get cheaper, chat apps become “the way people actually talk.” From **2015 ($4.7B)** to **2017 ($16.8B)**, WhatsApp’s growth is a straight-line climb—while SMS slides from **$92B (2015)** to **$76B (2017)**.

The storyline gets cinematic in **2018–2019**. WhatsApp rockets to **$28.5B (2018)** and **$42.0B (2019)**, while SMS sinks further: **$68B → $60B**. It’s not a cliff—it’s worse than a cliff: a slow-moving takeover. Even when RCS tries to modernize messaging (IP-based features), it grows like a door that won’t open fully—reaching only about **$9.2B by 2025**.

And while the West watches WhatsApp, WeChat proves the “OTT messaging wins” thesis in parallel—climbing through the same period to roughly **$47B by 2025**. By **2020–2021**, messaging usage is supercharged globally, and the gap widens: WhatsApp rises from **$58.5B (2020)** to **$77B (2021)**, while SMS slips from **$53B** to **$47B**.

By **2025**, the contrast is brutal: WhatsApp is estimated at **~$154B**, while global SMS messaging revenue is down to **~$28.5B**.

🔥 Question: In your country, did SMS die faster than you expected—or did it hang on longer than you thought?

facebook_caption:
Global texting tells a classic platform-war story. In 2011, SMS messaging revenue was estimated around $111B—an era where carriers monetized everyday communication directly. As smartphone adoption expanded and mobile data costs fell, Over-The-Top (OTT) messengers shifted usage away from carrier billing.

In this timeline comparison, WhatsApp’s estimated messaging value grows from near-zero in 2011–2012 to roughly $154B by 2025. Over the same period, global SMS messaging revenue compresses from about $111B to roughly $28.5B, illustrating how replacement happens through sustained behavior change rather than a single event.

The chart also contrasts other forces: WeChat acts as a parallel OTT success story, rising to around $47B by 2025, while RCS/IP messaging expands slowly to about $9.2B by 2025—showing why carrier-led modernization struggled to match the network effects and user expectations of OTT apps.

The most dramatic takeaway: the “default channel” moved. Once messaging became app-based, SMS became legacy utility instead of primary communication.

threads_caption:
Hot take: SMS didn’t “lose” — it got out-platformed. 😬

Look at this timeline: SMS revenue goes from about **$111B (2011)** to about **$28.5B (2025)**, while WhatsApp climbs from near-zero to **~$154B**. The switch wasn’t one day… it was years of people just choosing chat apps because they fit how we actually communicate.

WeChat proves the same pattern in its region, and RCS grows, but slowly (to ~**$9.2B by 2025**)—not enough to overturn OTT momentum.

What do you think—was your friend group the “early switchers” to WhatsApp/DMs, or did SMS hang on way longer than expected for you?
